text: Lesson 8 left Basic Auth with three real problems: the credential travels on every request, it never expires, and revoking it means changing a shared password. OAuth 2.0 is ServiceNow's standard modern answer to exactly that gap.

In the Client Credentials grant, the integration authenticates as itself, using only its client ID and client secret — no human user is involved at all. ServiceNow exchanges those credentials for a short-lived access token, then sends that token, not the underlying secret, on every call. This is the common choice for server-to-server work: a nightly sync, a scheduled job pulling data from a partner API.

The Authorization Code grant is different: it's used when the integration needs to act on behalf of a specific human user who has explicitly authorized that access. The user goes through a one-time consent step with the external provider, and the token that comes back represents that person's own authorization, not the integration's identity.

In ServiceNow, this is configured in two pieces. The OAuth Entity record holds the client ID, client secret, and token endpoint URL. The OAuth Entity Profile points at that record, selects the grant type, and is what actually gets attached to a REST Message's Authentication Profile — configure it once, and every REST Message using that profile inherits the setup.

Here's the real practical payoff: once that profile is attached, the developer's script doesn't manage tokens at all. ServiceNow requests a token the first time it's needed, caches it for reuse, and silently requests a fresh one when the cached token expires. A hand-rolled integration has to track expiry and catch failed calls itself — OAuth in ServiceNow removes that entire category of bugs.

Short-lived tokens, automatic refresh, and a grant type that matches whether a human is actually involved — that's why OAuth replaces Basic Auth for production work. Next up: Mutual Authentication and API keys, for the cases where even OAuth isn't the full answer.
